## 1. dmitrenko2026whymemorycomponents pages 2-4 (Context ID: pqac-00000073)

did not undergo events.
Section 6 proposes a decision instrument for architects.

2. Method

Population. We constructed a sample of 105 production-relevant open-source data-infrastructure and AI-
tooling projects from three documented sources used in parallel, plus six manual additions:

  • The DB-Engines popularity ranking top 50 as of May 2026 [DB-Engines, 2026] for relational, document,
      key-value, wide-column, time-series, graph, and search databases;
  • The CNCF graduated and incubating project list as of May 2026 [CNCF, 2026] for orchestration,
      observability, service mesh, and streaming categories;
  • A practitioner-curated landscape covering vector stores, orchestration frameworks, observability tools,
     and stream processing [Pracdata, 2024], filtered to projects with production deployments by named
      organisations. Pracdata is used only as an intake source for population construction; no event in the
      catalogue is sourced from it.


                                               2To these source-driven intakes we manually added six projects. Mem0 and Zep were added because they figure
prominently in the 2026 memory surveys discussed in Section 1, and both projects experienced catalogued
sustainability events within the analysis window [Mem0, 2026; Zep, 2025]; an analysis of memory-component
architecture would be incomplete without them. Percona, Linkerd, Vespa, and OpenObserve were added
because they appear in industry literature as Commercial-OSS or production-relevant alternatives within our
scope, and their inclusion ensures the conditional-rate denominators reflect the population more completely.
All six manual additions are flagged in the supplementary dataset.

Intake from the three documented sources overlapped substantially: many projects appear in two or all
three (for example, Apache Kafka in both DB-Engines and CNCF lists, or PostgreSQL across all three).
The final sample of 105 projects reflects deduplication and an inclusion filter requiring production-relevance
by January 2020 or by launch date if later. The sample spans launch years from 1995 to 2023 and covers
relational and document databases, key-value stores, vector and graph stores, search engines, message brokers,
observability tools, infrastructure-as-code, orchestration frameworks, service meshes, and AI tooling. We do
not claim the sample is representative of all open-source data infrastructure; we claim only that it covers the
visible commercial-and-near-commercial portion of the ecosystem most likely to be considered as memory
components. Rates reported in Section 3 should be read as descriptive statistics within this constructed
sample, not as ecosystem-wide population estimates.

Event definition. A license-or-sustainability event is any of:  (a) a license change away from an OSI-
approved license to a source-available license such as BSL, SSPL, FSL, the Elastic License, the Confluent
Community License, or a vendor-specific source-available licence; (b) the removal of features from an open-
source edition in favour of a commercial product, whether cloud-hosted or otherwise distributed; (c) the
deprecation of an open-source edition; (d) the archival of a repository without a maintained successor; or
(e) an acquisition followed within eighteen months by narrowing of the open-source surface. Adverse events
under (a)–(e) are counted against the originating project. Forks, reversals, thwarted attempts, and license
tightening between two OSI-approved licences are recorded in the catalogue as related entries and are not
counted as additional adverse events against any project: a fork is a community reaction to an event already
counted, a reversal does not net out the original event, a thwarted attempt is by definition not an event,
and a permissive-to-copyleft tightening within OSI-approved licences does not remove the project from the
open-source category. The dataset includes all five categories because volatility itself is the architectural
concern, but the rates in Section 3 use only adverse events (a)–(e) in the numerator.

The clarification of criterion (b) to “commercial product, whether cloud-hosted or otherwise distributed”
reflects an event class encountered after the first draft of this paper. Buoyant’s February 2024 removal of
stable Linkerd release artifacts from the open-source project, with stable releases available only through
the commercial Buoyant Enterprise for Linkerd distribution, fits criterion (b) in its structural form: the
open-source project is no longer feature-complete and production users must rely on a commercial product
to receive reliability guarantees. The original phrasing’s “cloud-only” was too narrow to capture this case
[Buoyant, 2024].

Coding. Each project is coded along three structural axes.

Governance  is single-vendor (one company holds copyright assignment and can unilaterally relicense),
foundation-governed (Apache Software Foundation, CNCF, Linux Foundation, or equivalent neutral body
holding trademark and aggregating contributions), or volunteer (an individual or small collective without
corporate copyright concentration, e.g. pgvector). An earlier draft of this work distinguished a “multi-
vendor” governance category for projects under foundation umbrella but funded by multiple independent
vendors; the data showed no analytical separation between this subgroup and foundation-governed projects
funded otherwise, and the category was collapsed.

Capital structure is coded into one of five categories. Venture-backed (primary funding from venture cap-
ital). Commercial open-source company (revenue-first business model around an open-source project, not
VC-primary; e.g. MariaDB, Percona).  Corporate-sponsored (engineers employed by a non-VC corporate
sponsor; e.g. PostgreSQL via EnterpriseDB and other vendors, Vespa via Yahoo). Foundation-funded (pri-
mary sponsorship from a foundation or distributed across multiple vendors under a foundation umbrella; in
this paper we group “foundation-only” and “foundation-plus-multi-vendor” into one category because the


                                               3data does not separate them in rate terms).  Volunteer (no corporate or foundation sponsor; individual
maintainers).

License is permissive (Apache 2.0, MIT, BSD, MPL, public-domain), copyleft (GPL, AGPL), source-available
at adoption (BSL, SSPL, ELv2, CCL, vendor-specific), or proprietary.

Coding edge cases. A small number of projects have mixed funding histories (e.g. began volunteer-led
and acquired corporate backing later). These were coded by their primary funding model at the time of
catalogue entry, with annotations in the supplementary dataset. Projects with combined coding (e.g. Volun-
teer/Foundation in the raw data) were rolled into the dominant category for the rate tables. The full mapping
from raw funding_model values in the supplementary CSV to the five canonical categories is documented
in the README of the dataset.

A specific coding choice worth flagging: Linkerd is coded as foundation-governed (CNCF graduated) with
venture-backed capital structure (Buoyant, the sole corporate steward employing all core maintainers, is
venture-backed). This combination, foundation governance with VC-backed single steward, is rare in the
sample (n=3) and is discussed as its own analytical cell in Section 4.

Sources. Every event in the catalogue is anchored to a primary source: a vendor blog post, an oﬀicial press
release, a license-file commit on GitHub, or a regulatory filing. Aggregator and SEO sources are excluded.

Data and code availability. The full catalogue is published as an open dataset on Zenodo under CC
BY 4.0: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20562988. The deposit contains projects.csv (the 105-project
population), events.csv (39 catalogued events with date, type, license-from, license-to, and primary-source
URL, of which 38 fall in the 2018 to May 2026 analysis window plus one pre-window reference entry), and
README.md documenting full file schemas, coding rules, summary statistics, and a version changelog.

Limitations. The sample is not random. It is biased toward projects with some commercial visibility, which
is the population most likely to be considered as memory components. Events affecting purely academic
or hobbyist projects are under-represented.  Conditional rates within sub-cells (for example, foundation-
governed venture-backed projects, with n=3) involve small numbers and should be read as orders of magni-
tude rather than precise estimates. Section 7 returns to these limitations.

Sample size in conditional cells. Several sub-cells in Section 3 are small: Commercial-OSS contains four
projects, Corporate-sponsored nine, Foundation-with-VC-steward three, Volunteer three.  Zero rates and
small-cell rates should be treated as orders of magnitude, not as estimates of population rates. We do not
report confidence intervals because the sample is not random a

## 2. dmitrenko2026whymemorycomponents pages 4-6 (Context ID: pqac-00000074)

 most likely to be considered as memory components. Events affecting purely academic
or hobbyist projects are under-represented.  Conditional rates within sub-cells (for example, foundation-
governed venture-backed projects, with n=3) involve small numbers and should be read as orders of magni-
tude rather than precise estimates. Section 7 returns to these limitations.

Sample size in conditional cells. Several sub-cells in Section 3 are small: Commercial-OSS contains four
projects, Corporate-sponsored nine, Foundation-with-VC-steward three, Volunteer three.  Zero rates and
small-cell rates should be treated as orders of magnitude, not as estimates of population rates. We do not
report confidence intervals because the sample is not random and the categorical coding involves judgement
(see “Event definition” above); rates are reported to one significant figure of resolution.

3. Base Rate and Conditional Rates

Across the sample of 105 projects, we catalogue 38 events between January 2018 and May 2026: 29 adverse
events plus 9 related entries (4 forks, 3 reversals, 1 thwarted attempt, 1 OSI-internal license tightening).
Twenty-five distinct projects experienced at least one adverse event over the window. One additional event
from January 2017, the MariaDB MaxScale move from GPL to BSL and the origin of the BSL framework
itself, is recorded in the catalogue as pre-window context and excluded from the rate calculations below.

Unconditional rate. Twenty-five of the 105 sampled projects experienced at least one adverse event over
the eight-year window (25 of 105, or approximately 24 percent).  All rates reported below are descriptive
rates within this constructed sample, not estimates of ecosystem-wide population rates; Section 7 returns to
sample selection and survivorship bias.

Annualized incidence. Adverse events per year by period:


                              Period          Events  Events per year

                            2018–2020       8        ~2.7
                            2021–2023       11       ~3.7



                                               4                              Period          Events  Events per year

                         2024–May 2026  10       ~4.2



Annualized incidence rose from approximately 2.7 events per year in the first sub-period to approximately
4.2 in the most recent, a roughly fifty-five percent increase. The trajectory is consistent with the rise of cloud
managed services as a commoditisation pressure on single-vendor open-source data infrastructure, with the
2024–May 2026 period extending the upward trajectory rather than plateauing. A longer follow-up window
would refine the trajectory further.

Adverse events by type. The 29 adverse events distribute as follows:


                   Event type                                      Count

                     License change to source-available                     16
               OSS feature removal in favour of a commercial product  4
                   Open-core split                                     3
                     Acquisition with narrowing or repository archive        3
                    Deprecation of open-source edition                    2
               New component released under restrictive license        1



License changes are the most frequent single type but do not dominate. Thirteen of twenty-nine adverse
events involve no license change at all: feature removal, deprecation, acquisition outcomes, and open-core
splits each produce production-architectural impact through mechanisms other than relicensing. The Mem0
v3 event of April 2026 (the motivating case in Section 1) falls in the feature-removal category, not the license-
change category. The Linkerd event of February 2024 is also in this category: the source code remains Apache
2.0, but stable production-grade release artifacts are no longer published by the open-source project [Buoyant,
2024].

To distinguish the three non-acquisition non-license categories: an open-core split introduces a separate
paid edition with features absent from the open-source one while leaving the open-source edition technically
functional (Meilisearch 2025, TimescaleDB 2018, YugabyteDB 2019). An OSS feature removal takes features
previously present in the open-source edition and moves them behind a commercial product (Mem0 v3, MinIO
GUI, Linkerd stable artifacts, InfluxDB v1-to-v2 transition). A new component released under a restrictive
license is a fresh product introduced by a vendor under non-OSI terms while the existing open-source project
remains under OSI terms (dbt Server). All three reduce the operational coverage of the open-source edition
relative to the commercial product, but through structurally different mechanisms.

Conditional rate by governance.


                    Governance          Sample   Projects with event  Rate

                      Single-vendor         61       23               ~38%
                     Foundation-governed  43       2               ~5%
                      Volunteer            1        0              0%



Two adverse events occurred under foundation governance. The first is the Hortonworks/Cloudera ecosystem
acquisition-and-deprecation of January 2019, with subsequent ecosystem narrowing.  The second is the
Linkerd February 2024 stable-release withdrawal: the project remains Apache 2.0 and CNCF-graduated,
but stable release artifacts moved behind the commercial Buoyant Enterprise distribution. The foundation-
governance category is heterogeneous — as Section 4 develops, the analytical separation that matters is
between foundation governance with a non-VC steward and foundation governance with a VC-backed sole
steward. Two further foundation-governance projects appear in the catalogue with non-adverse entries: the
Presto-to-Trino split of January 2019 (a governance dispute resolved by community migration to a renamed


                                               5project, coded as a fork rather than an adverse event for Presto itself) and the Synadia attempt of April
2025 to withdraw NATS from the CNCF, blocked by the CNCF charter, the only thwarted attempt in the
catalogue.

Conditional rate by capital structure.

                Capital structure                Sample   Projects with event  Rate

               Venture-backed                   53       24               ~45%
              Commercial open-source company  4        0              0%
               Corporate-sponsored (non-VC)     9        1               ~11%
               Foundation-funded                33       0              0%
                Volunteer                        3        0              0%


The Commercial-OSS row reflects a sample of four projects (MariaDB, Couchbase, Caddy, Percona) with no
adverse events in the catalogued window. Sample sizes for non-VC categories are small and the zero rates
should be read as orders of magnitude rather than precise estimates. A coding note: ScyllaDB, which moved
from AGPL v3 to a source-available license in December 2024, is coded as venture-backed (the company has
raised approximately $103M in cumulative venture financing from Bessemer, Eight Roads, TLV Partners,
and other investors) rather than Commercial OSS [ScyllaDB, 2024; TechCrunch, 2023]. The conditional
placement matters: the event fits the venture-backed pattern rather than the Commercial-OSS pattern, and
the row reflects that.

Conditional rate by license at population entry. The data does not show license type as the primary
signal. Among single-vendor permissive projects, approximately 39 percent experienced an adverse event;
among single-vendor copyleft projects, approximately 40 percent. The largest variation is by governance, not
by license. Among foundation-governed permissive projects the rate is approximately 4.7 percent; among
single-vendor permissive projects, approximately 39 percent. License type is doing little independent work
once governance is controlled for.

Combined cells. The interaction is not additive. The two-by-two cell of single-vendor governance and
venture funding produced approximately 46 percent of its members as event-experiencing projects (23 of 50).
The cell of foundation governance with non-venture funding produced approximately 2.5 percent (1 of 40).
The headline number for the paper is the approximately nineteen-fold differential between these two cells
(18.4× to one decimal place). Section 7 shows that this differential is invariant to the most contested coding
choice in the catalogue.

A third structurally distinct cell merits separate reporting: foundation governance with a venture-backed
sole corporate steward. The sample contains three such projects: Delta Lake (Databricks as sole steward),
Milvus (Zilliz as sole steward), and Linkerd (Buoyant as sole steward). Of the three, Linkerd experienced
an adverse event in February 2024. The cell rate is one in three. We treat this as a mechanism si

## 3. dmitrenko2026whymemorycomponents pages 6-8 (Context ID: pqac-00000075)

oundation governance with non-venture funding produced approximately 2.5 percent (1 of 40).
The headline number for the paper is the approximately nineteen-fold differential between these two cells
(18.4× to one decimal place). Section 7 shows that this differential is invariant to the most contested coding
choice in the catalogue.

A third structurally distinct cell merits separate reporting: foundation governance with a venture-backed
sole corporate steward. The sample contains three such projects: Delta Lake (Databricks as sole steward),
Milvus (Zilliz as sole steward), and Linkerd (Buoyant as sole steward). Of the three, Linkerd experienced
an adverse event in February 2024. The cell rate is one in three. We treat this as a mechanism signal,
not a rate estimate: with n=3 the binomial confidence interval is too wide for the point estimate to be
informative on its own, but the case is qualitatively important because it shows that foundation governance
is not a uniform structural backstop. The non-VC foundation cell rate of 2.5 percent and the VC-steward
foundation cell observation are structurally different conditions that the unconditional foundation rate of 4.7
percent averages over.

What the data does not show.  Sovereignty and data-residency concerns appear in the architectural
literature as compliance variables but did not surface as causes of any catalogued event. Sovereignty is a
meaningful architectural concern in its own right; it is not, in this dataset, a failure-predicting variable.

4. Mechanisms

The conditional rates establish that governance and capital structure correlate with event rates strongly
enough that they merit attention.  What follows asks what mechanisms could be behind the observed
pattern, and addresses a sub-mechanism that the small Foundation-with-VC-steward cell surfaced.


                                               6Single-vendor governance permits unilateral relicensing. Every catalogued license change followed
the same legal pattern. A single corporate copyright holder, having aggregated contributor copyright via
a CLA, exercised the right to ship subsequent versions under different terms. MongoDB held copyright
via its CLA and could move from AGPL to SSPL [MongoDB, 2018]. Elastic, HashiCorp, Cockroach Labs,
Lightbend, Redis Ltd, Grafana Labs, ScyllaDB, and Airbyte each used the same legal mechanism. The
license change is downstream; the upstream condition is the copyright structure. Distributed copyright —
PostgreSQL, the Linux kernel, OpenTelemetry — does not permit the same move because no single party
has standing to make it.

Foundation governance is associated with a structural backstop against relicensing. The NATS
attempt in April 2025 is the natural experiment. Synadia, the sole corporate steward of NATS, attempted to
withdraw the project from the CNCF and relicense it from Apache 2.0 to BSL. The CNCF charter Section
11a transfers trademark to the Linux Foundation on project donation, and the Linux Foundation retained
control of the project name. After several weeks of dispute, the parties settled: NATS core stayed Apache 2.0
under the CNCF, and Synadia retained the right to ship a separate BSL enterprise product [CNCF, 2025].
The structural difference between this case and the MongoDB or Redis cases is foundation membership with
trademark transfer. License integrity follows from trademark control.

Foundation governance’s backstop has bounds: distribution remains under steward control.
The Linkerd case of February 2024 is the structural complement to the NATS case. Linkerd has been CNCF-
graduated since July 2021. Apache 2.0 throughout. Buoyant is the sole commercial steward and employs
every core maintainer, a fact the company acknowledges publicly. In February 2024, Buoyant announced
that the Linkerd open-source project would no longer publish stable release artifacts; stable releases would
be available only through the commercial Buoyant Enterprise for Linkerd distribution [Buoyant, 2024]. The
source code remained Apache 2.0. The CNCF charter was not violated. The trademark backstop did not
engage because no relicensing was attempted. What changed was distribution: the production-grade artifacts
that organisations actually deploy moved from the OSS project to a paid commercial product.

The mechanism implied here is steward concentration interacting with venture pressure. When a foundation-
graduated project has a single corporate steward that employs all maintainers, the foundation charter blocks
relicensing but does not block the steward from deciding what the OSS project publishes versus what the
commercial product publishes. When that steward is venture-backed and faces the same commercial timeline
pressure as single-vendor venture-backed projects in Section 3, the pressure may find a distribution-side outlet
because the licensing-side outlet is closed. We do not claim this is proven by one event in a three-project cell;
we claim only that the Linkerd case is structurally consistent with the mechanism, and that the mechanism
is invisible if governance and capital structure are recorded but steward concentration is not.

The architectural implication: foundation membership alone, without attention to who employs the main-
tainers and how that employer is funded, may be an incomplete signal. The decision instrument of Section
6 is extended to six fields to reflect this.

Venture funding is consistent with monetisation pressure on a misaligned timeline.  Venture
funds have five-to-seven-year fund cycles. Production data infrastructure has multi-decade horizons. The
mismatch resolves in one of two ways. Either the project’s commercial steward generates enough revenue
from a managed-service or enterprise tier to satisfy investor return expectations, or the steward narrows the
open-source surface to protect that revenue against managed-service competition from cloud providers or
other commercial competitors. The catalogued events are consistent with the second option chosen at scale:
every major SSPL, BSL, or Elastic License adoption between 2018 and 2024 in the catalogue cited cloud-
provider competition as the precipitating cause [MongoDB, 2018; Elastic, 2021; HashiCorp, 2023; Redis,
2024].  Buoyant’s February 2024 announcement said the same thing in different terms: the problem was
the absence of revenue capture from users running stable Linkerd in production [Buoyant, 2024]. Section 7
returns to the causation-versus-correlation question explicitly.

License changes appear to be lagging indicators of revenue stress. ArangoDB moved from Apache
2.0 to BSL with v3.12 in early 2024, citing “evolving the licensing model for a sustainable future” [ArangoDB,
2024]. The framing of the announcement positions the change as a response to commercial pressure rather
than a precipitating cause. The pattern is similar for CockroachDB’s two license moves (Apache to BSL in


                                               72019, BSL to fully proprietary in 2024) and for ScyllaDB’s December 2024 transition to a source-available
licence [ScyllaDB, 2024], each occurring after multi-quarter periods of strategic repositioning visible in public
reporting. We do not claim a causal direction from this data; the pattern is consistent with license changes
signalling commercial pressure already in progress, rather than producing it.

Forks and reversals add a third dimension. Three of the largest 2018–2024 license events spawned
foundation-backed forks within months:  OpenSearch from Elasticsearch in April 2021, OpenTofu from
Terraform in August 2023, Valkey from Redis in March 2024.  Three more produced reversals.  Elastic
added AGPLv3 back in August 2024, Redis followed with AGPLv3 in May 2025, and InfluxDB returned
to MIT/Apache 2.0 in January 2025 [InfluxData, 2025]. The architectural lesson is that adverse events
open mobility paths when the underlying contributor and trademark structures allow it.  Architects who
picked components with credible fork-or-migration paths absorbed events at lower cost than those locked
into proprietary deployments.

5. Counterfactuals

Mechanisms gain force from cases that should fail under a naive reading of the data but do not.

PostgreSQL. Production-relevant since around 2000, license unchanged since the 1990s.  Single-vendor
governance is structurally impossible here because copyright is distributed across thousands of contributors
without CLA aggregation. The PostgreSQL Global Development Group is a coordinating body, not a copy-
right holder. Commercial vendors (EnterpriseDB, Crunchy Data, Supabase, Neon, Tembo) monetise around
the project with no path to relicense it.  Distributed copyright is the structural protection [PostgreSQL,
2026].

pgvector. A PostgreSQL extension under MIT, maintained by a single volunteer developer since 2021.
Production-critical for vector search across many AI deployments. No commercial entity, no venture backer,
no path to comme

## 4. fermigier2026valuecapturein pages 1-3 (Context ID: pqac-00000076)

                     Draft working paper · not peer-reviewed


   Value Capture in Commercial Open Source: Services,
  Funding Paths, and the FLOSS Value Network (Europe,
                          2026)

                      Stefane Fermigier (Abilian) · sf@abilian.com

   Draft working paper v0.7, 2026-09-23. Conceptual synthesis with a verified formal core; every proposi­
   tion has a proof, a numeric cross-check, and a Monte-Carlo robustness report; the funding-path reading
    is stated with the liquidity condition under which it holds; no firm-level estimate is reported.



                             Abstract


   Most accounts of the commercial open-source sector are written about its most visible minority,
   venture-backed product vendors relicensing against hyperscalers. This paper starts from the
   service majority, treating its share of the sector as a hypothesis to be measured. It builds on the
   value-network theory of FLOSS business models of Jullien, Viseur and Zimmermann (2025), in
   which a project’s value lies in managing the software flow and the 3A services (assurance, adap­
   tation, assistance) are sold to a segmented user base. It adds one axis the theory does not treat,
   the firm’s funding path, reduced in a two-period model to a discount parameter. Four verified
   results follow. Contribution to the project has a closed form that rises with patience, a reading
   that holds where the self-funded firm’s cash constraint is slack and is bounded by outside capital
   where it binds. Enclosure by relicensing has a unique patience threshold; a community able
   to fork shrinks the region where it pays, and erosion of the service margin or slowing growth
   widens it, which is when the visible relicensings happened. A heterogeneous population sorts
   into an open-service and an enclosed-product cluster on patience and conversion economics.
  The 2018 blueprint of the sector is revisited and the 2026 predictions are mapped to a survey
   instrument; no estimate is reported.

   Keywords: commercial open source, value capture, funding paths, venture capital, relicensing,
  FLOSS value network.
   JEL: L17, L86, L21, G24, O34.



                                         1. Introduction

The public account of commercial open source in the 2020s is a story of licensing wars:
Elastic, HashiCorp, and Redis abandoning permissive licenses to block cloud resale, and the
forks that followed. That story concerns a small, visible population. The economic mass of
the sector sits elsewhere, in firms that sell services around software they help maintain but
do not own, and that never face a relicensing decision at all. The theory this paper builds
on makes the same claim about the industry at large: the 3A services implemented in the
peripheral open-source models “account for the largest share of business activity” (Jullien,
Viseur & Zimmermann 2025, preprint p. 71; hereafter JVZ). This paper is about how those
firms capture value, and about the one strategic choice that most shapes it.
   The frame reads a FLOSS project as a value network, a configuration of actors who
create and capture value in the production of shared code (Morgan, Feller & Finnegan
2013), evolving through phases. It treats open-source companies as the participants who
sell services complementary to that code. Section 2 states the parts of that apparatus the
paper stands on: the stock-flow distinction, the 3A services, the user typology, the phase-by-
model map, and alienation management. Section 2.3 then places the model in the canonical
economics of open source, which explains why individuals contribute (Lerner & Tirole 2002)
and why firms participate (Bonaccorsi & Rossi 2003; von Hippel & von Krogh 2003). The
same economics explains which licenses projects adopt (Lerner & Tirole 2005), how the


                                      1public good is underprovided (Johnson 2002), and how a project evolves against commercial
competitors (Athey & Ellison 2014). None of it prices the contributor’s own cost of patience.
Within that frame the paper adds four things. The first is an axis the theory does not treat
(it classifies companies by their role in the project and is silent on how they are financed):
whether the firm is self-funded or venture-backed. In the European SME reality that is the
first-order predictor of which business model a firm can run, how it relates to the FLOSS
project, and whether it is exposed to the licensing and regulatory dynamics that dominate
the discourse. The next is a formal core that makes the axis operative: a two-period model
of the choice between the open service model and enclosure, proved, cross-checked, and
stress-tested. The third is the 2026 European institutional layer: SaaS delivery, sovereignty-
weighted procurement, and the Cyber Resilience Act, each read as a shift in the payoffs of
the theory’s models. The fourth is a bounding of the licensing and regulatory shocks to the
population they actually govern, with a claim-by-claim map to the measurement design that
will test the whole structure.

                                      12. Discussion

For theory. The paper extends the FLOSS phase model with a funding-path axis and
a European institutional layer, and bounds the licensing and regulatory dynamics to the
product-vendor population they govern. The formal weight of the paper rests on the axis:
the model of Sections 5 and 6 turns it into a closed-form contribution schedule, a threshold
characterization of enclosure, and deterrence and timing comparative statics. All of it is con­
ditional on a small model with assumptions that are stated and stress-tested. The theoretical
claim taken from the value-network account is that appropriability and the complementary
asset are coupled in open source: for vendors who capture a core, moving the license moves
the community, with opposite sign. The extension offers the theory a candidate answer to a
question it leaves open (why some editors enclose and others never do), in one parameter
the theory does not include: the patience induced by the firm’s capital structure.
   For managers. The first decision is the funding path, because it selects the game. A
founder on the self-funded path should build 3A-service depth, treat the core as shared
infrastructure, and read Proposition 1 as a return schedule. Patience raises the optimal in­
vestment in the project more than proportionally where cash does not bind (Remark 3); that
investment makes the service offer credible. A founder on the venture path should decide
early which complementary asset the firm will own before it needs to defend value, because
relicensing is survivable only for a firm that already owns one. The same founder should
prefer instruments that raise appropriability without breaking reciprocity before reaching
for a non-open license; the fork episodes of Section 10 are the cost side of that ledger.
   For policy. The population a European open-source policy most wants to sustain is
the self-funded service majority; a security mandate with a size-regressive fixed cost selects
against the very small firms and foundations at its base. If the goal is a resilient European
open-source sector, the mandate should be paired with instruments that flatten the fixed-cost
curve for small firms and foundations: mutualized compliance tooling, shared conformity
infrastructure, steward-regime clarity. This is a claim about instrument design; it reports
no measured outcome and credits no instrument with protection it has not been shown to
deliver.
   European policy analysis holds open source in two positions at once; the model shows
what reconciles them. The Commission’s critical-capacities study records in its SWOT that
“Open source is seen as a strength and a potential strategy to close gaps where Europe lags
behind global competitors, particularly the US and China. In areas like software, open source
could provide a more agile and collaborative route to innovation”. The same study’s depen­
dency inventory lists “Opensource standards (Kubernetes, Spark)”, “Orchestration Software
(e.g. Kubernetes, OpenStack) for Cloud”, “AI Frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch)”, and “Key
Blockchain Protocols (Ethereum)” among the EU’s technological dependencies, notes that
core protocols “are governed outside the EU, limiting influence over updates and standards”,
and observes that “In NGI, although much software is open source, many initiatives fail to
reach widespread adoption, and public institutions do not subsequently deploy or endorse
these home-grown alternatives” (European Commission 2026a). Both readings hold under a
condition this paper’s machinery states: an open license confers control on an adopter only
where the surrounding community can fork the project and sustain it afterwards, which is


                                      18the same capability 𝜙 that deters enclosure in Proposition 3. The license is the legal permis­
sion to fork; the capacity to exercise it is an asset that has to exist and be paid for. The study
names open source as a strategy without attaching an allocation to it: open source appears in
none of the four investment options’ budget grids and in no funding condition. The proposed
programme design contains no open-licensing requirement, no open-standards clause, and
no reuse obligation. Whether such conditions would move the fork capability of any project
is an empirical question that the design as described leaves untested.


                                     13. Conclusion

Open-source firms capture value by selling assurance, adaptation, and assistance around
code they help maintain; the shape of that value capture is set first by the funding path.
The theory supplies the machinery: value lives in the flow, the 3A services price access to
it, the typology shows who buys which, the phases say when each model is possible, and
alienation rights say who can enclose. This paper’s addition is the axis that selects among
the possibilities, now backed by theorems. Contribution rises with patience in closed form.
Enclosure is confined to impatient and conversion-rich firms below a unique threshold, forks
deter it at the margin, and margin erosion and maturity widen the region where it pays. The
population should split into two clusters if the reading is right. The 2018 blueprint is the
reference point and the 2026 European layer supplies the predicted shifts; the instrument
gives every claim its test. The drama of the licensing wars belongs at the edge of this picture,
and the economics of the service majority at its center. The claims are framed to be testable
and are left untested; the contribution of this draft is the structure and its measurement map.

The excerpt provides evidence for the industry and policy component of the requested topic, but it does not contain the Nagle (2018) learning-by-contributing study or a direct estimate of firm-level productivity. Nagle (2019) evaluates a French procurement law requiring government agencies to favor OSS over proprietary software. The design combines GitHub contribution data with difference-in-differences and synthetic-control analyses, using 20 OECD/EU countries as controls; an Italian law serves as a placebo because it was not enforced. The policy generated an estimated 50,000–57,000 additional French OSS contributions per month (nearly 600,000 annually), with 67–245 new contributors per month. Reported domestic spillovers include a 0.6%–5.4% annual increase in companies using OSS, a 9%–18% increase in IT startups, a 6.6%–14% increase in IT employment, and a 5%–16% decrease in software patents. These findings concern adoption/use of OSS and broader ecosystem outcomes, not vendor commercialization through an open-core model. The excerpt therefore supports distinguishing free-software adoption by firms or public agencies from firms selling proprietary extensions, hosted services, or other open-core complements; it offers no numerical estimate for that latter business model. {"answer": "# Commercial open source versus proprietary software: what the evidence shows

**Bottom line.** There is evidence that firms engaging with open-source software (OSS) can gain productivity, attract financing and become acquisition targets. There is much less evidence that **selling an open-core product, managed OSS service or dual-licensed product** produces higher valuations, faster revenue growth, more IPOs or better survival than selling proprietary software. Many studies measure *using or contributing to* OSS, not the licence of the firm’s principal revenue-generating product. These are different comparisons. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000042)

## Firm outcomes and business models

| Outcome | Empirical finding | What it does **not** establish |
|---|---|---|
| **Revenue and employment growth** | A 2011 master’s thesis by Chowdhury linked an older European software-firm survey to accounts. In regressions with hybrid firms as the reference group, the coefficients on *mainly OSS* and *mainly proprietary* were respectively **0.971 (SE 0.496)** and **0.874 (SE 0.264)** for log sales (366 observations); for log headcount they were **0.228 (SE 0.134)** and **0.551 (SE 0.276)** (299 observations). The thesis interprets mainly-OSS firms as growing more in sales but less in employees than mainly-proprietary firms. Crucially, the two coefficients’ separate significance against *hybrids* does **not** establish a statistically significant OSS–proprietary difference; no direct test of that difference is reported in the cited tables. The historical, selected sample also does not isolate modern SaaS or open-core firms. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000089) | A causal revenue-growth premium, or a reliable numerical percentage by which OSS outgrows proprietary companies. |
| **Profitability and productivity** | Singh *et al.* (2026) study **977 US high-tech firms, 2001–2025**, and estimate that adopting open product development through GitHub increased gross margin by approximately **4%–5% relative to nonadopters**, with specifications including staggered difference-in-differences and synthetic controls. Their mechanism analysis finds a positive indirect productivity effect when outside volunteers account for approximately **35%** of observed contributions; continued internal R&D is important. This covers high-tech firms adopting a development practice, **not** an identified cohort of commercial OSS vendors. Nagle’s *Open Source Software and Firm Productivity* (2019) is reported in the retrieved literature as finding productivity benefits conditional on complementary IT capabilities; its primary full text was unavailable here, so no precise Nagle coefficient is asserted. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000001) | That every OSS firm has higher margins, or that open-core licensing itself causes the reported gains. |
| **Financing and market value** | In a working-paper analysis linking **160,065 US startups** to GitHub, Conti, Peukert and Roche find that engagement with external OSS communities precedes an **at least 36% increase relative to the mean** in likelihood of first funding, versus matched startups. Engagement also precedes more product launches; the association is stronger for novel technologies and weaker in highly competitive markets. This is **funding probability**, not a valuation comparison, and GitHub engagement does not mean the startup sells OSS. An event study by Aksoy-Yurdagul (2025) uses **149 uncontaminated code-contribution announcements by 65 listed firms**: average abnormal returns are positive, with announcements explicitly seeking user insights associated with approximately **1.42% greater market value** than other contribution announcements. It measures announcement reactions, not an enduring open-core valuation premium. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000044) | Higher private-company valuations or superior long-run shareholder returns for OSS vendors versus otherwise comparable proprietary vendors. |
| **Acquisitions, IPOs and survival** | Vetter’s Crunchbase–GitHub study follows **67,794 young software firms**, of which **2,639 were acquired**; **111 IPOs** and **3,172 cessations of operations** are recorded. Firms whose employees worked on public OSS had a **higher acquisition hazard** than firms without observed OSS activity; more activity correlated with greater hazard. Within the OSS group, neither licence type nor attracting outside pull requests showed a significant acquisition association after controls. The principal acquisition model excludes firms that went public or ceased operations, using those outcomes as competing risks in a robustness analysis. This is an association with **participation**, not an estimate of OSS effects on exit *prices* or a finding that OSS firms survive longer. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041) | A demonstrated OSS advantage in IPO probability, acquisition proceeds or firm survival. |

**Why model distinctions matter.** An *open-core* firm offers an OSS core alongside proprietary paid features; *SaaS* sells hosting and operations and may or may not have an OSS core; *dual licensing* offers the same code under both OSS and commercial terms. Comino and Manenti’s account of dual licensing is **theoretical**, explaining when community feedback can make it commercially sustainable, not reporting a measured exit or growth advantage. A small, deliberately selected 2025 survey of **44 visible OSS developer tools** reports high funding among open-core/SaaS projects and warns explicitly about estimated private valuations, survivor bias and the absence of proprietary comparators. Its numbers should not be read as a population-wide valuation premium. Red Hat’s reported **$34 billion IBM acquisition** and HashiCorp’s reported **$6.4 billion IBM acquisition in 2025** demonstrate possible large exits, but two selected transactions cannot identify the effect of licensing; HashiCorp had already changed Terraform’s licence by the latter transaction. (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000063, pqac-00000064, pqac-00000066)

## Why firms participate—and what happens when licences change

Lerner and Tirole’s empirical study of nearly **40,000 SourceForge projects** associates licence choice with the intended audience: end-user projects tended toward more restrictive *OSS* licences, whereas developer-oriented and internet projects tended toward less restrictive ones; its corporate-origin analysis is more tentative. Their definition of “restrictive” concerns **copyleft within open source**—it must not be confused with SSPL or BSL’s restrictions on uses that make those licences non-OSS. Fosfuri, Giarratana and Luzzi’s study of **1995–2003 OSS product introductions** finds that greater software-patent stocks predict more OSS releases, software trademarks predict fewer, and hardware trademarks predict more in some categories. These are evidence about firms’ strategic selection and complementary assets, **not** proof of superior returns after release. Nagle’s separate analysis of a French OSS-favouring procurement policy reports increased contributions and IT startup formation compared with controls, but likewise does not compare the financial performance of open-core and proprietary vendors. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000092)

The four prominent relicensing episodes are distinct from choosing a copyleft OSS licence:

| Vendor change | Documented community or commercial outcome |
|---|---|
| **MongoDB, October 2018:** Community Server changed from AGPL to **SSPL** for subsequent releases. | This is an early instance of a vendor retaining source access while restricting commercial cloud-service use. The evidence assembled here does not establish a comparable sustained community fork or a causal effect on MongoDB revenue or valuation. (pqac-00000079, pqac-00000075) |
| **Elastic, announced January 2021; effective for Elasticsearch in February:** Apache 2.0 gave way to **SSPL/Elastic License**. | Amazon launched the Apache-licensed **OpenSearch** fork in April 2021. Elastic added the OSS **AGPLv3** option in August 2024; OpenSearch entered Linux Foundation governance in September 2024. In Foster’s measured periods, Elastic employees already supplied **over 95% of Elasticsearch lines added/deleted** before the change and continued to dominate afterwards. At OpenSearch, Amazon employees supplied **80% of additions** in its first year and **63%** in the measured year before its foundation transfer: diversity improved, but the fork was not initially independent of its corporate sponsor. (pqac-00000079, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015) |
| **HashiCorp, August 2023:** future Terraform releases changed from **MPL 2.0 to BSL**. | The Linux Foundation’s **OpenTofu** retained MPL 2.0. The manifesto had support from over **100 companies and 1,000 individuals**, but in its first measured year the main repository had **31 contributors at 11 organizations** making at least five commits; none had previously contributed to Terraform. HashiCorp employees dominated Terraform contributions both before and after relicensing. IBM’s subsequent acquisition cannot, without a counterfactual, be attributed to the licence change. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000086, pqac-00000066) |
| **Redis, March 2024:** BSD-3 gave way to **RSALv2/SSPLv1** for new Redis releases. | The BSD-3 **Valkey** fork launched under the Linux Foundation that month. In Foster’s 2024 observation windows, **12 non-Redis employees** made at least five Redis commits in the year *before* relicensing, versus **zero** in the following six months; their pre-change contributions were **319 commits**, compared with **164** from the six Redis employees meeting the same threshold. Valkey’s first six months had **29 such contributors at 10 companies**, **18** of whom had previously contributed to Redis. The windows differ in length, and these are contributor counts, not customer migration or financial performance. Redis subsequently offered **AGPLv3** with Redis 8 in 2025. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000068, pqac-00000087, pqac-00000088, pqac-00000075) |

The interpretation is **community reallocation, not demonstrated vendor financial harm or benefit**. Foster’s three-case GitHub study finds that foundation-backed OpenTofu and Valkey brought in more organizationally varied contributors than the original vendor-controlled projects, whereas a single-company fork remained more sponsor-dependent. Its samples cover only selected projects and main repositories; commit counts omit documentation, governance, users and actual deployments. A later peer-reviewed netnography by Foster and Germonprez finds a recurring sequence across the three cases: vendors **framed other firms’ use as free-riding**, made unilateral licence changes, and encountered organized fork responses. These cases were *selected because forks occurred*; they cannot estimate the probability that any licence change causes a fork. (pqac-00000068, pqac-00000069, pqac-00000070, pqac-00000071)

**Financial conclusion.** A contemporary analyst review summarized by Foster found **no clear evidence that relicensing improved the vendors’ financial results**; that is not a controlled finding that the effect is zero. Licence changes often coincide with cloud competition, business maturation and other strategic decisions. Neither the observed forks nor subsequent revenues or acquisitions isolate what would have happened under continued OSS licensing. Similarly, survival of a **project or fork** should not be substituted for survival of its **sponsoring firm**. The strongest supported claims are about financing access, productivity under specified conditions, acquisition *association*, and changes in contributor governance—not a general valuation, revenue-growth, IPO or survival premium over proprietary software companies. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000069, pqac-00000073)"}

# Commercial open source versus proprietary software: what the evidence shows

**Bottom line.** There is evidence that firms engaging with open-source software (OSS) can gain productivity, attract financing and become acquisition targets. There is much less evidence that **selling an open-core product, managed OSS service or dual-licensed product** produces higher valuations, faster revenue growth, more IPOs or better survival than selling proprietary software. Many studies measure *using or contributing to* OSS, not the licence of the firm’s principal revenue-generating product. These are different comparisons. (singh2026profitabilityofopensource pages 1-4, conti2021beefingitup pages 1-5, vetter2021acquisitionsandopen pages 111-114, comino2011duallicensingin pages 1-2)

## Firm outcomes and business models

| Outcome | Empirical finding | What it does **not** establish |
|---|---|---|
| **Revenue and employment growth** | A 2011 master’s thesis by Chowdhury linked an older European software-firm survey to accounts. In regressions with hybrid firms as the reference group, the coefficients on *mainly OSS* and *mainly proprietary* were respectively **0.971 (SE 0.496)** and **0.874 (SE 0.264)** for log sales (366 observations); for log headcount they were **0.228 (SE 0.134)** and **0.551 (SE 0.276)** (299 observations). The thesis interprets mainly-OSS firms as growing more in sales but less in employees than mainly-proprietary firms. Crucially, the two coefficients’ separate significance against *hybrids* does **not** establish a statistically significant OSS–proprietary difference; no direct test of that difference is reported in the cited tables. The historical, selected sample also does not isolate modern SaaS or open-core firms. (chowdhury2010theimpactof pages 47-52, chowdhury2010theimpactof pages 55-61, chowdhury2010theimpactof media 25e20b04) | A causal revenue-growth premium, or a reliable numerical percentage by which OSS outgrows proprietary companies. |
| **Profitability and productivity** | Singh *et al.* (2026) study **977 US high-tech firms, 2001–2025**, and estimate that adopting open product development through GitHub increased gross margin by approximately **4%–5% relative to nonadopters**, with specifications including staggered difference-in-differences and synthetic controls. Their mechanism analysis finds a positive indirect productivity effect when outside volunteers account for approximately **35%** of observed contributions; continued internal R&D is important. This covers high-tech firms adopting a development practice, **not** an identified cohort of commercial OSS vendors. Nagle’s *Open Source Software and Firm Productivity* (2019) is reported in the retrieved literature as finding productivity benefits conditional on complementary IT capabilities; its primary full text was unavailable here, so no precise Nagle coefficient is asserted. (singh2026profitabilityofopensource pages 1-4, singh2026profitabilityofopensource pages 33-35) | That every OSS firm has higher margins, or that open-core licensing itself causes the reported gains. |
| **Financing and market value** | In a working-paper analysis linking **160,065 US startups** to GitHub, Conti, Peukert and Roche find that engagement with external OSS communities precedes an **at least 36% increase relative to the mean** in likelihood of first funding, versus matched startups. Engagement also precedes more product launches; the association is stronger for novel technologies and weaker in highly competitive markets. This is **funding probability**, not a valuation comparison, and GitHub engagement does not mean the startup sells OSS. An event study by Aksoy-Yurdagul (2025) uses **149 uncontaminated code-contribution announcements by 65 listed firms**: average abnormal returns are positive, with announcements explicitly seeking user insights associated with approximately **1.42% greater market value** than other contribution announcements. It measures announcement reactions, not an enduring open-core valuation premium. (conti2021beefingitup pages 1-5, conti2021beefingitup pages 20-23, conti2021beefingitup pages 23-26, aksoy‐yurdagul2025generatingvalueby pages 1-2, aksoy‐yurdagul2025generatingvalueby pages 5-6, aksoy‐yurdagul2025generatingvalueby pages 8-9) | Higher private-company valuations or superior long-run shareholder returns for OSS vendors versus otherwise comparable proprietary vendors. |
| **Acquisitions, IPOs and survival** | Vetter’s Crunchbase–GitHub study follows **67,794 young software firms**, of which **2,639 were acquired**; **111 IPOs** and **3,172 cessations of operations** are recorded. Firms whose employees worked on public OSS had a **higher acquisition hazard** than firms without observed OSS activity; more activity correlated with greater hazard. Within the OSS group, neither licence type nor attracting outside pull requests showed a significant acquisition association after controls. The principal acquisition model excludes firms that went public or ceased operations, using those outcomes as competing risks in a robustness analysis. This is an association with **participation**, not an estimate of OSS effects on exit *prices* or a finding that OSS firms survive longer. (vetter2021acquisitionsandopen pages 103-106, vetter2021acquisitionsandopen pages 111-114, vetter2021acquisitionsandopen pages 114-117) | A demonstrated OSS advantage in IPO probability, acquisition proceeds or firm survival. |

**Why model distinctions matter.** An *open-core* firm offers an OSS core alongside proprietary paid features; *SaaS* sells hosting and operations and may or may not have an OSS core; *dual licensing* offers the same code under both OSS and commercial terms. Comino and Manenti’s account of dual licensing is **theoretical**, explaining when community feedback can make it commercially sustainable, not reporting a measured exit or growth advantage. A small, deliberately selected 2025 survey of **44 visible OSS developer tools** reports high funding among open-core/SaaS projects and warns explicitly about estimated private valuations, survivor bias and the absence of proprietary comparators. Its numbers should not be read as a population-wide valuation premium. Red Hat’s reported **$34 billion IBM acquisition** and HashiCorp’s reported **$6.4 billion IBM acquisition in 2025** demonstrate possible large exits, but two selected transactions cannot identify the effect of licensing; HashiCorp had already changed Terraform’s licence by the latter transaction. (comino2011duallicensingin pages 1-2, pandey2025theeconomicsof pages 1-8, pandey2025theeconomicsof pages 8-13, pandey2025theeconomicsof pages 23-27)

## Why firms participate—and what happens when licences change

Lerner and Tirole’s empirical study of nearly **40,000 SourceForge projects** associates licence choice with the intended audience: end-user projects tended toward more restrictive *OSS* licences, whereas developer-oriented and internet projects tended toward less restrictive ones; its corporate-origin analysis is more tentative. Their definition of “restrictive” concerns **copyleft within open source**—it must not be confused with SSPL or BSL’s restrictions on uses that make those licences non-OSS. Fosfuri, Giarratana and Luzzi’s study of **1995–2003 OSS product introductions** finds that greater software-patent stocks predict more OSS releases, software trademarks predict fewer, and hardware trademarks predict more in some categories. These are evidence about firms’ strategic selection and complementary assets, **not** proof of superior returns after release. Nagle’s separate analysis of a French OSS-favouring procurement policy reports increased contributions and IT startup formation compared with controls, but likewise does not compare the financial performance of open-core and proprietary vendors. (lerner2005thescopeof pages 1-5, fosfuri2008thepenguinhas pages 1-2, fosfuri2008thepenguinhas pages 10-12, nagle2019governmenttechnologypolicy pages 1-6)

The four prominent relicensing episodes are distinct from choosing a copyleft OSS licence:

| Vendor change | Documented community or commercial outcome |
|---|---|
| **MongoDB, October 2018:** Community Server changed from AGPL to **SSPL** for subsequent releases. | This is an early instance of a vendor retaining source access while restricting commercial cloud-service use. The evidence assembled here does not establish a comparable sustained community fork or a causal effect on MongoDB revenue or valuation. (fermigier2026valuecapturein pages 22-23, dmitrenko2026whymemorycomponents pages 6-8) |
| **Elastic, announced January 2021; effective for Elasticsearch in February:** Apache 2.0 gave way to **SSPL/Elastic License**. | Amazon launched the Apache-licensed **OpenSearch** fork in April 2021. Elastic added the OSS **AGPLv3** option in August 2024; OpenSearch entered Linux Foundation governance in September 2024. In Foster’s measured periods, Elastic employees already supplied **over 95% of Elasticsearch lines added/deleted** before the change and continued to dominate afterwards. At OpenSearch, Amazon employees supplied **80% of additions** in its first year and **63%** in the measured year before its foundation transfer: diversity improved, but the fork was not initially independent of its corporate sponsor. (fermigier2026valuecapturein pages 22-23, foster2411thenewdynamics pages 8-11, foster2411thenewdynamics pages 11-15) |
| **HashiCorp, August 2023:** future Terraform releases changed from **MPL 2.0 to BSL**. | The Linux Foundation’s **OpenTofu** retained MPL 2.0. The manifesto had support from over **100 companies and 1,000 individuals**, but in its first measured year the main repository had **31 contributors at 11 organizations** making at least five commits; none had previously contributed to Terraform. HashiCorp employees dominated Terraform contributions both before and after relicensing. IBM’s subsequent acquisition cannot, without a counterfactual, be attributed to the licence change. (foster2411thenewdynamics pages 11-15, foster2411thenewdynamics pages 15-18, foster2026freeridingandrebellion pages 14-14, pandey2025theeconomicsof pages 23-27) |
| **Redis, March 2024:** BSD-3 gave way to **RSALv2/SSPLv1** for new Redis releases. | The BSD-3 **Valkey** fork launched under the Linux Foundation that month. In Foster’s 2024 observation windows, **12 non-Redis employees** made at least five Redis commits in the year *before* relicensing, versus **zero** in the following six months; their pre-change contributions were **319 commits**, compared with **164** from the six Redis employees meeting the same threshold. Valkey’s first six months had **29 such contributors at 10 companies**, **18** of whom had previously contributed to Redis. The windows differ in length, and these are contributor counts, not customer migration or financial performance. Redis subsequently offered **AGPLv3** with Redis 8 in 2025. (foster2411thenewdynamics pages 15-18, foster2411thenewdynamics pages 18-21, foster2024thenewdynamics media 6119b756, foster2024thenewdynamics media b2337e5f, dmitrenko2026whymemorycomponents pages 6-8) |

The interpretation is **community reallocation, not demonstrated vendor financial harm or benefit**. Foster’s three-case GitHub study finds that foundation-backed OpenTofu and Valkey brought in more organizationally varied contributors than the original vendor-controlled projects, whereas a single-company fork remained more sponsor-dependent. Its samples cover only selected projects and main repositories; commit counts omit documentation, governance, users and actual deployments. A later peer-reviewed netnography by Foster and Germonprez finds a recurring sequence across the three cases: vendors **framed other firms’ use as free-riding**, made unilateral licence changes, and encountered organized fork responses. These cases were *selected because forks occurred*; they cannot estimate the probability that any licence change causes a fork. (foster2411thenewdynamics pages 18-21, foster2411thenewdynamics pages 21-23, foster2026freeridingandrebellion pages 1-2, foster2026freeridingandrebellion pages 24-25)

**Financial conclusion.** A contemporary analyst review summarized by Foster found **no clear evidence that relicensing improved the vendors’ financial results**; that is not a controlled finding that the effect is zero. Licence changes often coincide with cloud competition, business maturation and other strategic decisions. Neither the observed forks nor subsequent revenues or acquisitions isolate what would have happened under continued OSS licensing. Similarly, survival of a **project or fork** should not be substituted for survival of its **sponsoring firm**. The strongest supported claims are about financing access, productivity under specified conditions, acquisition *association*, and changes in contributor governance—not a general valuation, revenue-growth, IPO or survival premium over proprietary software companies. (foster2411thenewdynamics pages 3-6, foster2411thenewdynamics pages 6-8, foster2411thenewdynamics pages 21-23, dmitrenko2026whymemorycomponents pages 2-4)

contexts.context: This excerpt provides background on potential commercial advantages and risks of firms engaging in open source software (OSS), but it does not present a quantitative matched comparison of commercial OSS firms versus proprietary-software firms across valuation, revenue growth, IPO or acquisition probability, survival, or related outcomes. It cites Nagle (2018a) as finding that firms active in nonpecuniary/free OSS are associated with significant positive value-added returns, but gives no sample size, effect magnitude, confidence interval, standard error, or comparison design. Reported benefits include faster user adoption, access to talent and external innovation, development-cost or sourcing-cost reductions, and increased demand for complementary products and services. The excerpt also emphasizes important qualifications: OSS can make monetization difficult, expose intellectual property, reduce competitive advantage, create community-management challenges, and lead to project forks after acquisition. Copyleft obligations and poor OSS tracking may reduce the value of acquired intellectual property; an industry study is cited reporting that 47% of companies lacked formal processes for tracking OSS code, although this is not an outcome comparison between OSS and proprietary firms. The author concludes that OSS engagement may increase target attractiveness by reducing uncertainty, but may alternatively signal resource scarcity or create commercialization and control risks. Thus, the passage is relevant for framing hypotheses and qualifications, but supplies almost none of the requested comparative statistics.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes Chowdhury’s empirical study of how business models affect the growth performance of open-source-software (OSS) firms. It does not report the requested quantitative comparison between commercial OSS firms and proprietary-software firms, nor does it provide estimates for valuation, revenue growth effects, IPO or acquisition probabilities, survival, statistical uncertainty, or matched-sample comparisons. The study uses the 2004 ELISSI survey, which sampled OSS firms supplying OSS-based products or services in Finland, Germany, Italy, Portugal, and Spain. Of 6,000 firms contacted, 915 responded; the empirical accounting sample contains 378 firms from Finland, Italy, Portugal, and Spain, because German firms could not be matched using VAT codes. Firms were retained when accounting performance data were available for at least two financial years, with financial data covering 2004–2009 and drawn from AMADEUS and ORBIS. The dataset includes sales, employees, tangible and intangible assets, total assets, salaries, business model, and organizational characteristics. The sample is heterogeneous but predominantly small: roughly 75% had 2003 sales of €2 million or less, 56.5% employed 10 or fewer people, and 91.7% had total assets below €1 million. The author cautions that OSS firms constitute a hidden population without an official census, so the sample is not representative. The excerpt ends before presenting econometric specifications, comparison groups, coefficients, standard errors, or conclusions.

contexts.context: Vetter’s excerpt describes a quantitative study comparing young software firms active in open source software (OSS) with software firms not active in OSS, focusing primarily on acquisition likelihood and timing rather than valuation, revenue growth, IPO outcomes, or survival as broad firm outcomes. The design combines Crunchbase firm and acquisition data with GitHub development data and uses survival models to estimate differences in acquisition probability. It also examines whether OSS engagement characteristics—overall commit activity, ability to attract community contributions, and license focus—are associated with acquisition probability, and uses ordinary least squares models to study how an acquirer’s prior OSS engagement relates to acquisition timing. The reported dataset includes firms founded between 2011 and 2018: 12,597 were identified as OSS-active, and 2,639 firms in the sample were acquired; the excerpt also states a total of 67,793,894 firms founded in that period, although the surrounding text is truncated. No coefficient estimates, effect sizes, confidence intervals, p-values, or matched-comparison results appear in this excerpt. Important qualifications are that GitHub data are available only after 2010, the acquisition sample covers 2014–2018, and the study does not observe firms that were rejected because of OSS involvement. Thus, the excerpt supports identifying Vetter’s sample and empirical strategy, but not extracting quantitative effects or statistical uncertainty.

It contains no sample sizes, estimated effects, standard errors, confidence intervals, p-values, or matched-comparison methodology. Conceptually, proprietary software is described as reducing customer-perceived risk through standardized documentation, maintenance, updating, and responsibility, while open-source software can lower the ratio of fixed to total costs but may increase perceived risk, particularly for small new entrants. contexts.context: The excerpt reports an observational analysis of 44 open source developer tools from 2020–2025, rather than a direct matched comparison of commercial open source firms against proprietary software firms. It claims that business-model choice is more predictive of commercial outcomes than GitHub adoption metrics, with projects controlling service-layer infrastructure achieving substantially higher valuations than community-funded alternatives with comparable star counts. Open Core plus SaaS projects reportedly had median funding above $40 million, while community-only alternatives had zero venture funding. Examples include Supabase at a reported $5 billion valuation and Vercel at $9.3 billion, but the excerpt does not provide effect sizes, confidence intervals, regression coefficients, revenue-growth measures, IPO or acquisition probabilities, survival estimates, or formal uncertainty statistics. The authors explicitly qualify the findings: associations may reflect founder-selection effects, market timing, investor sentiment, category selection, and other confounders; the 2020–2025 period included unusually favorable funding conditions; and survivor bias likely overstates commercial success because failed ventures are less documented. Consequently, these findings are useful as descriptive background but do not supply the rigorous cross-firm valuation, growth, exit, or survival comparisons requested, nor do they establish causality.

contexts.context: A forthcoming *Information Systems Research* study (Singh et al., 2026) provides longitudinal firm-level evidence, using 977 U.S. high-tech firms (2001–2025), 323,634 GitHub events, and 44,147 repositories. Firms adopting open-source product development experienced an average **4%–5% gross-margin increase** versus peers, robust to staggered DID, synthetic-control, instrumental-variable, and dynamic-panel methods. Labor productivity partially mediated this effect, but the indirect benefit became positive only when external volunteers contributed approximately **35%** of development activity. High-profitability configurations consistently included R&D intensity. The authors note that prior research was mostly theoretical, qualitative, or cross-sectional, lacking longitudinal profitability evidence.

They classify licenses as unrestrictive (BSD), restrictive (LGPL/copyleft), or highly restrictive (GPL/“viral”). End-user, game, and desktop projects more often use restrictive licenses, while developer-oriented, Internet, and commercial-operating-system projects are less restrictive. A smaller exploratory sample suggests corporate spin-out projects choose more restrictive terms. Findings support the theory that licensing reflects both licensor incentives and contributor-community appeal; the authors caution that implications for commercial software are limited.

contexts.context: Fosfuri, Giarratana, and Luzzi (2008) study OSS commercialization, not firm outcomes versus proprietary companies. Using firms’ OSS product announcements in specialized press (1995–2003), they find three robust relationships: large software-patent stocks increase likelihood of releasing OSS; large software-trademark stocks decrease it; large hardware-trademark stocks increase it. They argue OSS reduces secrecy and imitation barriers, so firms profit through complementary assets, proprietary components/licenses, trademarks, hardware, distribution, integration, and network effects. Novell’s Linux-related revenue was $44 million in Q1 2005—15% of sales.

contexts.context: Research finds vendor relicensing-to-fork chains understudied and rare. Robles & González-Barahona recorded only 13 forks before 1998; forks are disruptive, parallel, and often maintained by different people with little interaction (Businge et al., 2022). XFree86’s 2004 non-GPL-compatible relicensing led to X.org’s endorsement and XFree86’s abandonment. Since 2018, about 18 vendor projects reportedly moved from OSI licenses to source-available terms (“open washing”). Riehle links this to product maturity, competition, and investor ROI. Yet RedMonk’s Stephens (2024) found no financial evidence that relicensing improved vendors’ results; Elastic later restored AGPLv3 (2024). Corporate participation can sustain projects, but dominant firms can endanger them.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides theoretical background from Vetter (2021), not the exact empirical acquisition results requested. It states that prior acquisition research finds acquisition likelihood rises with technological similarity and complementarity, that acquirers may prefer similar R&D pipelines but complementary product portfolios, and that other positive correlates include network position and national-cultural similarity. For OSS specifically, the text lists possible benefits—faster user adoption, talent attraction, complementary-product demand, lower development or sourcing costs, and access to ideas and capabilities—and possible downsides, including difficult monetization, loss of intellectual-property control, competitive imitation, community-management challenges, project forks, copyleft and compliance risks, and OSS activity signaling resource scarcity. Vetter emphasizes that the literature had not yet established the OSS–acquisition intersection and therefore could not make clear predictions about whether OSS activity increases or decreases target attractiveness. No sample sizes, comparison groups, coefficients, standard errors, confidence intervals, financial estimates, or explicit empirical limits for Vetter’s OSS acquisition analysis appear in this excerpt. The excerpt also contains no findings for Chowdhury (2010), Fosfuri et al., Lerner and Tirole, or Singh et al. (2026), so those requested results cannot be extracted here.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports Vetter’s empirical findings on OSS activity and firm acquisitions. Using a dataset combining Crunchbase firm/acquisition data with GitHub OSS-development data, the study examines young firms founded between 2011 and 2018 and applies ordinary least squares models to acquisition timing/hazard. Of 67,793,894 firms, 12,597 were identified as OSS-active; 2,639 firms were acquired, including 808 OSS-active firms at acquisition. Relative to firms not active in OSS, OSS-active firms had a higher acquisition hazard. Among OSS-active firms, greater OSS activity was also associated with a higher acquisition hazard. After controlling for potentially confounding variables, the study found no significant evidence that license choice or the ability to attract outside contributions affected acquisition probability. For acquisition timing, targets active in OSS were acquired significantly earlier by acquirers that were themselves OSS-active than by acquirers not active in OSS. The excerpt does not provide coefficient estimates, effect sizes, standard errors, confidence intervals, or model tables. Its language is associational (“associated”), so the reported evidence does not establish that OSS activity causally increases acquisition likelihood or accelerates acquisition. The passage mentions robustness checks but does not report their specifications or results. It also does not contain findings on Chowdhury, Fosfuri et al., Lerner and Tirole, or Singh et al.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides one substantive empirical result relevant to the question: Fosfuri et al. (2008), “The Penguin Has Entered the Building: The Commercialization of Open Source Software Products,” examines the likelihood that a for-profit firm releases a commercial OSS product. contexts.context: Fosfuri, Giarratana, and Luzzi study firms’ OSS product announcements from 1995–2003 and estimate product-introduction models for two categories, OPSYS and APP. Their results support a positive association between software-patent stocks and OSS commercialization: in the robustness-check table, the software-patent coefficient is positive and statistically significant across the reported models, generally about 0.003–0.015 for APP and 0.011–0.015 for OPSYS, with alternative specifications producing larger coefficients (0.159–0.499). Software trademarks have a negative and generally significant association with OSS introductions, with coefficients commonly around −0.007 to −0.021 for OPSYS/APP and much larger negative estimates in the final specification. Hardware trademarks are positive for OPSYS (roughly 0.031–0.034 in several models) but mostly insignificant for APP; hardware patents are negative for OPSYS and not generally significant for APP. The authors interpret this as evidence that patents help appropriate OSS returns, proprietary software brands create cannibalization or reputation concerns, and hardware trademarks provide complementary assets. The study’s limits include observational announcement data, a 1995–2003 period, product-introduction outcomes rather than financial performance, and results that vary by product category and specification. This excerpt does not provide findings for Vetter (2021), Chowdhury (2010), Lerner and Tirole, or Singh et al. (2026).
